title: How to Call Rust from Node.js with napi-rs
summary: Build Node.js native add-ons with Rust and napi-rs. Export functions, objects, and async tasks, then package prebuilt platform binaries for npm.
body_markdown:
To call Rust from Node.js with napi-rs v3, scaffold a project with` npx @napi-rs/cli new` , mark Rust functions with` #\[napi\]` , run the build, and` require` the generated` index.js` like any other module.


Maybe a hashing loop is slowing your event loop, or you need a native library and don’t want to go back to fighting` binding.gyp` . The[C++ add-on route through node-gyp](https://blog.openreplay.com/node-gyp-troubleshooting-guide-fix-common-installation-build-errors/) works, but every user’s machine ends up needing Python and a compiler. This guide builds a working Rust add-on, adds an object return type and an async function, and shows how prebuilt binaries get to users through npm.


## Key Takeaways


- napi-rs compiles` #\[napi\]` -annotated Rust into a` .node` binary and also generates a JavaScript loader (` index.js` ) and TypeScript declarations (` index.d.ts` ).
- A napi-rs v3 project needs Rust 1.88+, plus Node.js ^20.17.0, ^22.13.0 or 23.5.0+ for the CLI. That CLI requirement is separate from the Node versions the finished add-on supports.
- An exported` async fn` needs the` async` or` tokio_rt` feature on the` napi` crate, and it is typed as returning a` Promise` .
- A napi-rs package ships as a root package plus one optional package per platform, so the people who install it never need Rust.


## What Is napi-rs?


napi-rs is a framework for building Node.js native add-ons in Rust. You mark Rust functions with` #\[napi\]` , and the build produces a` .node` binary, a JavaScript loader, and TypeScript declarations generated from the Rust signatures.


napi-rs sits on top of[Node-API](https://nodejs.org/api/n-api.html) , Node’s ABI-stable C interface for add-ons. Because the interface is ABI-stable, a binary compiled against one Node-API level can generally load in later Node.js releases that still provide that level, without a rebuild. Callers import the add-on like a normal module and get typed autocomplete.


## napi-rs vs WebAssembly: Which Should You Use?


Choose napi-rs when your code runs on the server and needs the file system, native threads, or an existing native library. Choose Wasm when the same code also has to run in the browser. napi-rs and Wasm aren’t mutually exclusive: napi-rs can[produce an optional WASI build](https://napi.rs/docs/cli/napi-config) , and the generated loader can fall back to it.


napi-rs WebAssembly node-gyp C++


File system and native threads Yes Limited, depends on host Yes


Links existing native/C libraries Yes Only if compiled to Wasm Yes


Per-platform builds required Yes, built in CI No Yes, or compiled at install time


Optional WASI build with loader fallback Yes N/A No


Toolchain the user needs at install None None Often Python and a C++ compiler


Generated TS types Yes Depends on tooling No


Which option is faster depends on the workload, so benchmark your own hot path. To go further with Wasm, read about[running high-performance code with Wasm](https://blog.openreplay.com/running-high-performance-code-wasm/) and[publishing WebAssembly packages for npm](https://blog.openreplay.com/publishing-webassembly-packages-for-npm/) .


## Create a napi-rs Project


To create a napi-rs project, run` napi new` through the` @napi-rs/cli` package. The[getting-started docs](https://napi.rs/docs/introduction/getting-started) list the prerequisites: Rust 1.88 or newer, Node.js ^20.17.0, ^22.13.0 or 23.5.0+ for the CLI, Git, and a C linker. The Node versions your finished add-on runs on are a separate question, governed by the Node-API level it compiles against.


With the Yarn template:


```text
yarn   dlx   @napi-rs/cli   new   hash-rs
cd   hash-rs
yarn   install
yarn   build
```


With the pnpm template:


```text
pnpm   dlx   @napi-rs/cli   new   hash-rs   --package-manager   pnpm
cd   hash-rs
pnpm   install
pnpm   build
```


Only Yarn and pnpm templates are supported. The[napi new prompts](https://napi.rs/docs/cli/new) ask for the path, package name, Node-API level, targets, license, and whether to generate a CI workflow. The scaffold contains these files:


- **` src/lib.rs`** : your exported Rust functions.
- **` Cargo.toml`** : declares` crate-type = \["cdylib"\]` and the napi-rs v3 crates. Keep the versions it writes, and check it for the Node-API feature level you picked.
- **` build.rs`** : generated and required. It calls` napi_build::setup()` and must stay at the crate root, so don’t edit it.
- **` package.json`** : the` build` script runs` napi build --platform --release` . The` napi` block holds your config:


```text
{
"  napi  "  : {
"  binaryName  "  :   "  hash-rs  "  ,
"  targets  "  : [  "  x86_64-apple-darwin  "  ,   "  aarch64-apple-darwin  "  ,   "  x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu  "  ,   "  x86_64-pc-windows-msvc  "  ]
}
}
```


Copy the field values from your generated file. Each build writes` hash-rs.<platform>.node` (for example` hash-rs.darwin-arm64.node` ), along with` index.js` and` index.d.ts` .


Code written for napi-rs v2 won’t work unchanged. If you copied from an older tutorial, check it against the[v2 to v3 migration guide](https://napi.rs/docs/more/v2-v3-migration-guide) :


v2 v3


` napi.name`` napi.binaryName`


` napi.triples` flat` napi.targets` array


` napi.package.name`` napi.packageName`


` napi create-npm-dir`` napi create-npm-dirs`


` JsObject` ,` JsFunction` typed v3 APIs; old types are behind the unsafe` compat-mode` feature


## Write a CPU-Heavy napi-rs Function


Export a Rust function by adding` #\[napi\]` to a` pub fn` . Add a hashing crate first:


```text
cargo   add   sha2
```


Then replace` src/lib.rs` with this napi-rs v3 code:


```text
use   napi_derive::  napi;
use   sha2::  {  Digest  ,   Sha256  };


/// Hash `input` with SHA-256, `rounds` times.
#[napi]
pub   fn   sha256_rounds  (  input  :   String  ,   rounds  :   u32  )   ->   String   {
let   mut   data   =   input  .  into_bytes  ();
for   _   in   0  ..  rounds  .  max  (  1  ) {
data   =   Sha256  ::  digest  (  &  data  )  .  to_vec  ();
}
data  .  iter  ()  .  map  (  |  b  |   format!  (  "{  :02x  }"  ,   b  ))  .  collect  ()
}
```


The function rehashes its own output` rounds` times, which is the kind of tight loop that blocks a JavaScript thread. Rust` String` maps to a JS string and` u32` maps to a JS number. The hex encoding is a manual loop, so it doesn’t rely on version-specific formatting in` sha2` . Rebuild with` yarn build` . The function appears in` index.d.ts` under the camelCase name` sha256Rounds` .


Call it from a CommonJS file such as` try.cjs` :


```text
const   {   sha256Rounds   }   =   require  (  '  ./index.js  '  )
console  .  log  (  sha256Rounds  (  '  hello  '  ,   1  ))
// 2cf24dba5fb0a30e26e83b2ac5b9e29e1b161e5c1fa7425e73043362938b9824
```


The[simple-package walkthrough](https://napi.rs/docs/introduction/simple-package) uses the same build-then-require loop.


## Return Objects and Promises


In napi-rs, use` #\[napi(object)\]` to return plain JS objects, and` async fn` to return Promises. According to the[Object concept page](https://napi.rs/docs/concepts/object) , every field of a` #\[napi(object)\]` struct must be` pub` . The struct can then serve as an argument or a return type, and its value is copied when it crosses the boundary.


For[async functions](https://napi.rs/docs/concepts/async-fn) , turn on the` async` feature (or` tokio_rt` ) on` napi` , and add Tokio for file I/O:


```text
[  dependencies  ]
# keep the features the scaffold wrote, and append "async"
napi   = {   version   =   "  3  "  ,   features   = [  "  async  "  ] }
```


```text
cargo   add   tokio   --features   fs
```


Append the following to the existing` src/lib.rs` , which already imports the` napi` macro and` Sha256` . The` ?` after` fs::read` works because napi converts` std::io::Error` into its own` Error` type.


```text
use   napi::bindgen_prelude::*  ;
use   tokio::  fs;


#[napi(object)]
pub   struct   FileHash   {
pub   path  :   String  ,
pub   bytes  :   u32  ,
pub   sha256  :   String  ,
}


#[napi]
pub   async   fn   hash_file  (  path  :   String  )   ->   Result  <  FileHash  > {
let   content   =   fs::  read  (  &  path  )  .  await  ?  ;
let   sha256  :   String   =   Sha256  ::  digest  (  &  content  )
.  iter  ()
.  map  (  |  b  |   format!  (  "{  :02x  }"  ,   b  ))
.  collect  ();
Ok  (  FileHash   {   bytes  :   content  .  len  ()   as   u32  ,   path  ,   sha256   })
}
```


An exported napi-rs` async fn` runs on a Tokio runtime that napi-rs manages. In the generated types,` hashFile` returns a` Promise` that resolves to a` FileHash` object, and a Rust` Err` becomes a rejected Promise.` async fn` fits I/O work like this. For long pure-CPU jobs, napi-rs provides[AsyncTask](https://napi.rs/docs/concepts/async-task) , which runs work off the main thread.


## How Do You Publish a napi-rs Package to npm?


People who install a napi-rs package don’t need Rust. A napi-rs package ships as a small root package plus one optional package per platform, and the package manager installs only the binary whose` os` ,` cpu` , and (where relevant)` libc`[package.json fields](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/configuring-npm/package-json#os) match the machine.


Here is what happens at install time:


1. The user installs the root package.
2. The package manager skips optional packages whose` os` ,` cpu` , or` libc` fields don’t match.
3. The matching platform package installs a prebuilt` .node` file.
4. ` index.js` finds that binary and loads it.


` napi.targets` lists every platform you ship. A local` napi build` compiles only one target, though: your host, unless you pass` --target` . The other binaries come from the generated GitHub Actions workflow. Its publish job runs` napi create-npm-dirs` to create one npm package directory per target, then moves each built artifact into the matching directory before publishing.


Each target needs its own package name, so use an[npm scope](https://docs.npmjs.com/about-scopes) :


```text
{
"  name  "  :   "  @yourscope/hash-rs  "  ,
"  optionalDependencies  "  : {
"  @yourscope/hash-rs-darwin-arm64  "  :   "  1.0.0  "  ,
"  @yourscope/hash-rs-linux-x64-gnu  "  :   "  1.0.0  "  ,
"  @yourscope/hash-rs-win32-x64-msvc  "  :   "  1.0.0  "
}
}
```


## Conclusion


You now have a Rust add-on that Node loads like any other module, with generated types and prebuilt per-platform binaries, so your users never install a Rust toolchain. Next, move your slowest CPU-bound function into` src/lib.rs` , measure it against the JavaScript version on real inputs, and push a tag to let the generated CI build every target.


For more Rust reading, see[Getting Started with Loco, Rust’s Answer to Rails](https://blog.openreplay.com/getting-started-loco-rust-rails/) .


## FAQs


What is the difference between async fn and AsyncTask in napi-rs?


An async fn runs on the Tokio runtime that napi-rs manages and suits async I/O. AsyncTask runs Task::compute on Node's libuv thread pool and suits bounded blocking or CPU-bound work. Both return a Promise to JavaScript. The libuv pool is shared with Node's file system, DNS, and crypto work, and an AbortSignal can cancel an AsyncTask only before its compute step starts.


What happens when Rust code panics inside a napi-rs function?


Without the catch_unwind option, a Rust panic that reaches the Node-API boundary aborts the whole Node.js process instead of throwing. Mark the function with #\[napi(catch_unwind)\] to turn the panic into a JavaScript Error built from the panic payload. This needs the default unwind panic strategy, and it can't catch an aborting panic. For expected failures, return Result instead: an Err from a synchronous function is thrown as a JavaScript Error.


Do napi-rs add-ons work in Bun and Deno?


Bun support is best effort. The napi-rs repository runs a latest-Bun CI job, but Bun failures do not block napi-rs releases, so test your own add-on in Bun. Deno native add-ons are not in the napi-rs source CI matrix, and the napi-rs docs warn against assuming Deno support from Node-API compatibility alone. The optional WASI fallback also has known gaps in both runtimes.


Which Node-API level should a napi-rs add-on target?


The Node-API level sets the oldest runtime your add-on can load on. A binary built against Node-API level N can generally load on later Node.js releases that still provide level N, with no rebuild for each Node major. A higher level gives access to newer Node-API functions but raises that floor. Functions added after your chosen level are not available.
